title: Chapter 34 – Night Visitors
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian; Old Hu]

"Again," Su Qinghe says. "And this time do not breathe like you are afraid of the ground."

It is the second week of summer, an hour before dawn, and the quarry is a bowl of blue shadow. Mist lies in the bottom of it. Mother stands on the old loading ramp with her arms folded, a gardener's hat pushed back on her head, and at the foot of the ramp Jian is trying to walk across forty paces of loose gravel without being heard.

He is wearing the Still Water Veil. It is not the difficulty. The Veil is a still pond, a held breath, a way of folding his Qi until it reads as less than it is. He has worn it every day for four years. The difficulty is that a veil which holds a boy still does not hold a boy moving. Each footstep sends a ripple through the surface, and every ripple is a small bright flaw in the dark, visible to anyone who knows how to look.

"Your left heel," Mother says. "It speaks every time it lands."

"I am not putting weight on it."

"You are putting weight on it so carefully that it shouts." She comes down the ramp, light and unhurried, and he feels the Veil wrap around her as she passes, and she makes no sound at all. "Here is the shape of the thing. The Veil hides Qi. It does not hide a body. Walk, and the body disturbs the air and the stone, and the stone passes the disturbance on to the Qi, and the Qi reveals you. So you do not walk through the quiet. You walk with it."

"The step has to be inside the Veil."

"The step has to be part of the Veil." She stops in front of him and puts two fingers on his sternum. "Here is what I have been trying to say. You fold your Qi on the inside, the way you fold a cloth. Now fold the step. Each foot, before it lands, takes a little of that fold with it. It lands inside the stillness, not on top of it."

It is an elegant idea, and he can see at once what is wrong with it. A fold costs Qi. A fold carried through every step costs Qi on every step. He does the arithmetic as he stands there, the small cold calculation he has made a thousand times: twice the usual expenditure, maybe a little more. Eleven minutes before the first stage runs dry.

He tries. He lets his weight come down on the left heel, and as it comes he draws the fold along the sole of his foot, a thin sheet of quiet, like laying a cloth on the stone before he steps. The heel lands. There is no sound. He feels the ripple start and watches it die in the fold before it spreads.

Mother's two fingers leave his chest. "That," she says, "is the first time you have ever surprised me on purpose."

"It is costing me a lot."

"Of course it is. Everything good costs a lot." She walks back up the ramp, and her voice comes down to him over her shoulder. "I call it Veil Step. Yellow grade. A rogue's art, from the islands. A dozen of us used it to walk through a sleeping town in the dark, and half of us were caught anyway, because a Foundation cultivator's sense does not read the Qi. It reads the seam where the fold meets the world. It sees the stitching." She stops at the top. "Do not use it where an FE might be standing. And do not use it for more than a few minutes. Your reserve is not as deep as you think."

"I know my reserve, Mother."

"I know you know it." She turns. In the blue dark her face is hard to read. "That is what frightens me."

* * *

By the time summer has fully arrived, the granary has become a small, ugly, thriving machine.

It runs on a pattern so simple that Jian is almost embarrassed by it. Lin Kai and Lin Dong cart spoil down from the head of the quarry in wicker baskets, two hundred baskets a day. A sluice of diverted spring-water carries the gravel through a trough with a lip, where the heavier flecks fall into riffles and the light rock goes on its way. Hu's forge takes what remains. A bellows, a crucible, a stone mold, an ingot the size of a brick. Each brick is stamped with the hammer-over-wave mark, gray and lumpy and ugly, and it weighs more than it should.

It also stinks. The whole east wall stinks. The women of the household have started tying cloths over their faces when they pass the granary, and Old Nan has called it the Devil's Kitchen to Hu's face, a name which Hu has adopted with pleasure.

Fourteen ingots a week. Two stones apiece from the Willow Ford refiner, who asks no questions of a famous fool. By the end of spring the treasury had recovered what the autumn court took, and by midsummer it will have grown beyond it. The tribute is paid. The Pavilion's security is paid. The clan eats.

But the money is the smaller part of it. What Jian watches, each evening from the stool beside the anvil with a bowl of soup in his lap, is the thing the old man does not say.

Hu has changed. It is a small change, and Jian is not certain anyone else has seen it. The hand that holds the hammer is a little steadier. The shoulders are a little straighter. For fifteen years Hu has lived like a man waiting for a sentence to be carried out, and in the last six months he has begun, haltingly, to act as though he might be around when the year ends.

He wants something to build, Jian thinks. Even something ugly.

He does not say it. He drinks the soup.

* * *

It is Hu who gives him the warning, on a night when the moon is a thin white paring over the east ridge.

They are alone in the granary. The forge is banked, and a heap of fresh ingots lies cooling on the sand. Hu sits on an upturned bucket with his wine jar between his knees, the pinned sleeve hanging loose, and his eyes are not drunk. They have not been drunk for a long time. It has become a habit, like a shirt he wears.

"The ingots will be noticed," he says.

"They have already been noticed. The refiner at Willow Ford has been asking where we find them."

"Not the refiner. The other ones." Hu taps the jar with his left hand. "I have been walking the east wall at night, as old men do. In the last three weeks I have found five different places where someone has lain in the grass and watched the granary. One of them left a spent tallow candle with the Red Ridge mark scratched into the butt. Not a good mark. A careless one. Someone who wanted it to be found."

Jian says nothing.

"A careless mark is a message. It says: we are watching, and we are not hiding. The question is why." The old man's eyes are steady. "In my experience, it means somebody has already decided to do something, and is giving you the courtesy of a warning so that, afterward, they can claim it was a mistake."

"Zhao Bei."

"Zhao Bei does the arithmetic. Heng gives the orders. Between them they have worked out that a refinery on the Lin east wall, producing spirit iron out of a hill they thought was dead, is a small problem today and a large one in three years." He lifts the jar, looks at it, sets it down. "I would rather it were a small problem a few weeks from now than a large one then. Which means I would like to be ready."

"A trap."

"A trap." Hu shows his teeth. "I told you once that I never said anything about traps."

"You did."

"I was lying."

* * *

It takes nine days to build.

Jian does not call it a plan. He calls it a list. A list is a thing you can add to, and cross off, and nobody can say afterward that you meant to hurt anyone. It has ten items. The first is a six-pin snare under the loading path from the quarry to the granary yard, where any stranger coming in over the east wall would have to cross. The second is a four-pin binding laid under the granary's side door. The third is a long sheet of stretched paper behind the forge, treated with a thin film of capsaicin concentrate, ninety-one percent, enough to blind a man for an hour in a closed room.

The fourth is the sleeping place.

"Not the loft," Hu says, when he sees it. "The loft is where they will look."

"The rafters over the door." Jian points. A black beam runs across the top of the side doorway, sunk in shadow, a hand's breadth wide. "From there I can see the yard, the path to the sluice and the whole length of the forge floor. If one comes through the door, I am above him."

"And if he looks up?"

"He will not." He keeps his voice level. "I will be wearing the Veil, and the Veil Step, and I will not be moving."

Hu looks at him for a long time. In the weak light the old man's burnt face is unreadable. "You are ten years old," he says at last.

"Yes."

"I am going to be very angry about this for the rest of my life."

"I know."

"Good." Hu looks away, and picks up his hammer, and begins to examine it with great attention. "Put a quilt in the rafter. Your mother will not forgive me if you catch a chill."

* * *

They come on the fourth night of the dark moon.

Jian has been in the rafter since the hour of the dog. He lies on a quilt with a bag of dried plums at his elbow and a small knife in his right hand, a palm-length blade of gray-black spirit iron with a horn handle, and the six pins of the snare strung out in his mind like beads on a thread. He is the only thing in the granary that is awake. Hu lies on a pallet by the cold forge, mouth open, snoring richly, a wine jar spilled at his side. The jar is a prop. The snoring is not. Hu snores for real when he has been drinking, and the old man had drunk precisely enough to make it convincing.

At the second hour after midnight, Father's Boundary Alarm slip on the east wall warms against his chest.

He does not move. It has been warm for a quarter of an hour, a slow, faint, impersonal heat. The slip detects crossings, not intentions. Someone has stepped over the line of the wall, and then, a long while after, someone else.

Two.

He lets his sense reach outward, past the granary wall, into the dark. It is four hundred paces of reach and forty of depth, and at the edge of the forty he feels a thing that does not belong. It is damp and cold. It has no weight. It rolls toward him over the grass like breath on a mirror, silver-gray, spreading, soundless.

Mist.

It is very good mist. He had been warned of it. A rogue named Ke Tian, a Qi Refining eighth-stage, from the river towns south of Willow Ford, known in a certain kind of tavern as the Fog. He has a reputation for killing cultivators in their own bedrooms without their servants hearing. He does it with illusion: a bank of mist that carries sound and scent and false shapes, so that a man who thinks he is fighting three attackers is in fact fighting one.

The mist reaches the wall. It climbs it, slow as a cat. It spills over the top and begins to run down the inside of the yard, and as it runs it carries something with it. Figures. A line of men in gray cloaks, walking toward the granary at a steady pace, their faces blank and shadowed. A dozen. Twenty.

Jian reads them with the part of him that does not feel fear.

```
[ARK-7 :: Scan]
Target: 21 figures, east yard
Real material composition: 1
Remainder: water vapor and Qi-light. No tissue. No bone.
```

One.

He finds him by the sound. It is not a sound at all but a patch of silence, a place in the mist where the damp air does not carry the scrape of leather or the shift of a weight. The real man is walking in the middle of his own decoys, a little behind the front rank, in a long gray cloak with the hood drawn up. A thin man, middle height, light on his feet. In his right hand is a short curved blade.

Qi Refining, eighth stage. Mist Veil Art. He is smelling for the sleeping place.

The second one has not yet come over the wall.

Jian waits.

He lets the figures approach, and walk on silent feet to the yard's edge, and stop. He lets Ke Tian lift his free hand, and sweep it through the air, and say something so soft it is only the shape of a word. The false line breaks, and flows around the granary, and gathers at the closed doors. Every one of them lifts a hand to the wood.

It is, Jian thinks, a very beautiful piece of work.

Now come in. Come in through the side door, where there is nobody to see.

He has laid the whole structure so that it wants to be walked into. The side door is slightly ajar. A ribbon of lamp-glow falls through it onto the floor, and inside the glow there is nothing but a sleeping drunk and a silent forge. It is the most inviting door in the world.

Ke Tian takes the side door.

He comes in slowly, slipping through the gap without touching it. His boots make no noise on the stone. His eyes sweep the room from left to right: the anvil, the banked coals, the heaped ingots, the sleeping old man with his wine jar. He sees the ingots and does not look at them. He sees the old man and he smiles, very faintly, under the hood.

He steps across the threshold. He steps on the third paving stone from the jamb.

Jian closes his hand.

Four.

Four pins fire together in the stone, silver light running between them in a square, and the man's body goes rigid in the middle of a step. He does not cry out. A man in the grip of a binding does not have the breath for it. His blade is half raised and his cloak hangs forward from his shoulders, and the hood falls back, and the face beneath it is thin and pale and astonished.

The binding lasts four heartbeats against a Qi Refining eighth-stage. Jian has measured it. Four heartbeats is long enough.

He drops.

It is not a leap. It is a controlled falling, with the Veil Step wrapped around his feet and the fold carried through each stride, and he lands on the stone behind the rogue's left shoulder without a single sound. The knife is already moving. It goes in under the back of the skull, at the place where the cord of the spine meets the base of the brain, and it goes in all the way, and the gray-black blade does exactly what Hu made it to do.

Ke Tian's eyes widen, and then go blank.

All at once, the mist outside the granary flinches. The false figures stutter, and flicker, and unravel into rags.

Jian holds the body up. He does not let it fall. It is a good deal heavier than he expected. He lowers it onto the stone with a great and terrible care, as though it might wake, and when it is on the ground he steps back, and wipes the knife on the dead man's own cloak, once, twice, three times.

His hands are steady.

That is the thing that frightens me, he thinks. My hands are steady.

He does not have time to think any further.

* * *

The second one comes through the roof.

He has been waiting on the thatch above the forge, a heavy man named Pock, a fire-thrower with a scar down the left side of his face. He had come over the wall behind Ke Tian, and he had been waiting for the Fog's signal, and when the mist unraveled he knew at once what it meant. A Qi Refining seventh-stage. Not so fine a craftsman as his partner. Not so careful. But he has lived thirty years doing a thing that kills people, and he is quick.

The roof tiles split. He drops through the hole in a rain of dust and wood-chips, and he lands in the center of the forge floor with a ball of orange fire already forming in his right hand, and he throws it.

It is not aimed at Jian. It is aimed at the ingot pile.

Jian does not think. He moves.

He has the second Royal Spirit Chain in his left hand before he knows he has reached for it, one of the three Father drew for him in the winter, a long paper slip with a single unbroken stroke, and he throws it as the fireball leaves the man's hand. The chain unspools in the air. Pale gold loops around the rogue's wrist, his forearm, his throat. The fireball bursts a hand's breadth short of the pile, and the shockwave throws Jian flat against the wall with his teeth rattling.

Six breaths. The chain holds six.

Pock roars. It is a raw sound, full of pain and fury. He tears at the golden links with his free hand, and they burn him, and he does not stop. The skin of his fingers blisters and splits. Two breaths. Three. He gets his fingers under the loop at his throat.

Jian is already on his feet. He is bleeding from somewhere over his left eye and the ringing in his ears is enormous, but his mind is perfectly clear. He sees where the man's weight is. He sees the quilt, and the wine jar, and the glow of the forge. And he sees the thing that Hu told him, on the first day of the pins, in a voice he can still hear.

A man who is angry looks at the thing that hurt him. A man who is afraid looks at the door. A man who is clever looks at both.

Pock is angry.

He runs.

Not at the man. At the forge. He slides to his knees at the edge of the cold sand-bed and slaps the wooden lid off the bucket there, the one Hu filled with quenching brine, a full pail, ten liters of heavy salt water, and he throws it. Not at the man's face. At his feet. At the fine gray sand around his boots.

Salt water on hot sand makes a flash of steam like a cough. The sand is not hot, but the brine is cold, and the half-melted slag in the shallow trough beneath is, and where the two meet there is a hiss and a gout of white vapor that boils up between the rogue's knees. Pock jerks back. He cannot see. His boot comes down, and the sole finds the second paving stone from the door, and Jian closes his hand again.

Six.

The snare takes him around the ankles. Six pins fire in a hexagon, and the rogue's legs lock, and he falls forward onto his knees with his arms held out in front of him, and the Royal Spirit Chain tears loose from his throat and floats, a hand's breadth from his face, dissolving into gold dust.

"Boy," he says. His voice is thick. "Boy. I did not mean—"

It is not true, and both of them know it.

Jian crosses the floor in four steps. The knife goes in beneath the ear, and the rogue's head drops forward, and he does not say anything more.

* * *

It is very quiet in the granary afterward.

The mist has gone. The false figures have dissolved into the dark. A thin line of dawn has not yet begun to show in the east, and the only light is the dull orange glow of the banked forge, throwing the shadows of two dead men across the floor.

Jian sits on an overturned bucket with the knife across his knees and his head between his hands. He is not shaking. He has been waiting to shake, and it has not come, and that is a cold, strange fact that he will have to think about, later.

Behind him, a voice says, "Well."

He does not need to turn. He knows the smell of wine and old smoke, the creak of that left knee. Hu has risen from the pallet. He walks slowly across the floor, in his stockinged feet, and stands for a time looking at the two bodies. Then he looks at the ceiling, where the hole gapes in the thatch. Then, at last, at the boy.

"Pock had a scar down his face," he says, very mildly. "I have heard of him. A man who burned a caravan at Salt Ridge. I did not think he was so good."

"He was good."

"He was very good, and you are a boy of ten with a quilt." Hu bends, with a grunt, and turns the dead man's face to the light. "And the Fog. The Fog. I would not have wanted to take him in his own mist, with one hand and a rod, and he is killed with a pin in a doorway." He straightens. "You did it exactly the way I would have told you not to, and exactly the way that works."

"I am sorry."

"For what?"

Jian does not know how to answer that. He looks at his hands.

"Good." Hu's voice is very gentle. "Keep being sorry. I stopped when I was thirty. It was a mistake." He sets his hand on the boy's shoulder, the single hand, heavy and hard and warm. "Now listen. You are going to go and wash. Quickly, before your mother gets here. And when she asks, you were in the rafters when the alarm rang, and you slept through the whole thing."

"She will not believe it."

"She will not ask. That is her gift." The old man's mouth tightens. "I killed them. Two rogues in the night, hired by Zhao Bei, killed by a drunken old artificer who happened to have laid a few pins for his own amusement and who was lucky. That is what we will say. Everyone on this hill will believe it, because everyone on this hill has been wanting to believe something like it since midsummer. Say it back to me."

"You killed them."

"Louder."

"You killed them. You laid the pins. You were lucky."

"Good boy." Hu lets go of his shoulder. "Now go."

* * *

He does not go to the well at once.

There is a task he has to do first, and he does it in the cold shed behind the granary, among old crucibles and broken molds, with a lamp turned down to a bead of light.

It is on the floor beside the first body where it has fallen, half hidden under the dead man's cloak: a small gray pouch on a cord, the size of a fist. He had seen the shape of it through the cloth on the first night he scanned the rogue, and had known at once what it was. A storage pouch. They are common among cultivators of the eighth stage and above, and he has never owned one in his life. He picks it up with great care, because he knows what a dead man's pouch may do.

```
[ARK-7 :: Scan]
Item: Storage pouch (Yellow grade, medium tier)
Space: ~2.1 cubic meters
Owner mark: Ke Tian (blood-keyed, residual)
Contents: not itemized — requires owner key or Separation
Note: residual blood-mark will signal to the owner's kin or sect on contact with live Qi.
```

Owner mark, residual. He sits very still. If he opens it with his own Qi, it will announce itself to anyone who knew the dead man. That is the nature of a blood-key. He has seen what a blood-key does to a hand that is not its owner's.

Separation. He lays a palm on the pouch.

```
[ARK-7 :: Separation]
Target: blood-key residue (organic, 0.4 g)
Cost: CE 4
Proceed?
```

He thinks about the number. He has scanned and measured and counted every point of Creation Energy that has come to him in ten years, hoarded each of them like a miser. There are twenty-nine to go before the door. Four is a seventh of that. It is a heavy price for a bag.

Two cubic meters. Pills. Spirit iron. A place that nobody knows about.

He says yes.

The pouch warms in his hand. A fine red thread rises out of the cord, thin as a spider's silk, and hangs a moment in the lamplight, and breaks. The knot on the pouch's mouth goes slack. Beneath the grain of the leather he can feel, faintly, the shape of what lies inside, and it does not tell him what it is.

He does not open it. Not tonight. He ties it under his tunic against his ribs with a loop of twine, and he covers the lamp, and he goes out into the cold gray start of the morning with the knife wiped clean and his hands steady.

At the edge of the yard, Mother stands in the first light.

She has come over the wall from the guardhouse, her hat in her hand. She has seen the broken roof. She has seen, through the open door, the two dark shapes on the granary floor, and Hu bending over them with a lamp. She stands there very still. Her face in the dawn is the color of old bone.

Then she looks at him.

Jian does not say anything. He stands with the blood drying under his fingernails and the small hard weight of the pouch against his ribs, and he looks back at her, and he waits for the question.

Su Qinghe takes a long breath. She takes a handkerchief from her sleeve, and crosses the cobbles, and kneels, and wipes his face. Slowly, thoroughly, as she did when he was three.

"You have a cut over your eye," she says. "Come to the kitchen. I will clean it."

That is all. She takes his hand and leads him across the yard, past the wall, past the well, and she does not look back at the granary once.

* * *

An hour after sunrise, Hu sits on the granary step with the sleeves of his robe stained brown and a cup of tea he is not drinking.

The guards have come, and gone, and come back. Wenshi has seen the bodies and said nothing for a long time. Father has stood in the yard, in his house robe, looking at the broken roof, and Hu has told him the story exactly as agreed, and the Patriarch has listened with a face like a closed door and said only: "I thank you, Old Hu. I would be grateful if you would find the boy and tell him to eat something."

The yard is quiet. A servant is sweeping.

And in the stillness, with nobody near him, Hu opens the left hand he has kept clenched since dawn.

In it lies a scrap of damp paper, torn from the inner lining of a dead man's cloak. It is cheap stuff, a drawing in blood-red ink, hasty and half smeared. A crude map. A square for the granary. A line for the east wall. And beside it, in a trembling hand, a mark that Hu knows better than any other mark in the world. A droplet, falling into a pool, ringed by three small lines.

Beneath it, two words.

The smith. Alive.

He reads it twice. Then, slowly, with the great weariness of a man who has been running for fifteen years and has only just noticed that the road does not end, he closes his hand around the paper and crushes it.

It is not Zhao's mark. It is the mark of the Blood Shadow's Pool stage, a Foundation elder's, older and far more patient.

A Pool mark, he thinks. Someone of the Pool has found me at last.
